AI is driving a historic global earnings boom.

The proportion of countries where earnings are estimated to decline YoY is down to ~5%, its lowest level since 2021.

This is also comparable to the lows seen in 2004-2006 and 2010-2011, following the recovery from the 2008 Financial Crisis.

By contrast, this reading spiked above 90% during the Financial Crisis and the 2020 pandemic.

Meanwhile, the MSCI All-Country World Index (MCWI) is up 13.4% year-to-date, and trading near its all-time high.

The index is on track for its 4th consecutive double-digit annual gain, following a +20.7% increase in 2025, +15.7% in 2024, and +20.2% in 2023.

The global bull market is broadening.

tweets.text:
US homebuyers are quitting.

There were an estimated +51.3% more home sellers than buyers in July, the 2nd highest level on record.

This percentage has doubled over the last 2 years.

By comparison, an all-time high of +51.8% was recorded in December 2025.

This comes as the number of active homebuyers fell -2.5% MoM, to 966,752, the lowest on record.

At the same time, the number of sellers declined -0.3% MoM to ~1,462,921, the lowest reading in a year, but the decline was far smaller than the drop in buyers.

As a result, ~80% of major US metros are now buyer's markets, led by Miami, where sellers outnumber buyers by +154%.

Further downward pressure on home prices is likely coming.

🇺🇸 Anthropic seems to have built one of the best models available but its customers don’t appear willing to pay much more to use it - FT

➡ Will the company building the best model actually be the one capturing the most value?

1️⃣ At Anthropic, Fable 5 remains relatively underused by businesses despite being positioned as its most capable model. A large share of spending is still going toward cheaper models and it seems companies are not necessarily looking for the best model but for a model that is good enough at the best possible price. If a slightly weaker model can do 95% of the job at half the price, the trade-off becomes obvious, and that raises a much broader question around how much companies are actually willing to pay for each additional unit of “intelligence".

🤔 OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and xAI are spending enormous amounts to stay at the technological frontier but there is no guarantee that their pricing can rise as quickly as their costs. You can therefore end up with a product that keeps getting better while its unit price keeps falling. Great for the customer, much less obvious for the margins of the model providers. Moreover, as performance gaps narrow, price, latency, distribution, integrations and reliability increasingly matter more. Commoditization, isn't it ?

2️⃣ On the other hand, corporate clients’ API spending on OpenAI is now growing slightly faster than Anthropic’s quarter-to-date. We still need to be cautious because the quarter is not over but it shows that OpenAI does not necessarily need to have the best model across every benchmark. It just needs to offer the best combination of performance, price and distribution.

✅ All this can be bearish for the labs’ pricing power while remaining very bullish for compute. If the cost of a query falls by 50% but companies multiply usage by 10 as they deploy agents across their organizations, total compute consumption can still explode.

To me, if this trend is confirmed with future model generations, the scarce resource may ultimately not be intelligence itself, but infrastructure, distribution and the ability to turn that intelligence into genuinely profitable use cases.

*FT link: https://t.co/ayJbuWKKxA

The SEC just gave crypto its first US fundraising ladder, copied straight from a 90-year-old rule.

Regulation Crypto Assets, proposed Aug 18, sets three caps: $5M startup, $20M Tier 1, $75M Tier 2. The top two match Reg A. Tier 2 adds audited financials and preempts state registration, one federal path instead of 50.

Projects that raised offshore for lack of a US rulebook now have one, with a safe harbor that ends a token's security status once its network is built. Comments close Oct 20.

You don't rebuild the American cattle herd by importing foreign beef and intentionally selling it below the market price American ranchers receive.

That's exactly the opposite of the incentive structure one would use to encourage domestic supply growth.

More supply + below-market foreign competition → lower domestic beef prices → lower cattle prices → weaker margins/incentives for American ranchers → less domestic supply
